title: Everything You Wanted To Know About Your Memory
header: The surprising reasons you forget—and what actually helps memory
content:
Memory allows us to learn, store information, and recall experiences. Although the brain has an enormous capacity for learning, memory is not perfect and can be influenced by attention, practice, health, and aging.

How Memory Works

  • Sensory memory: Briefly holds information from your senses for a fraction of a second to a few seconds.
  • Short-term memory: Temporarily stores a small amount of information for about 15 to 30 seconds unless it is actively rehearsed.
  • Long-term memory: Stores knowledge, skills, and experiences for extended periods, sometimes for a lifetime.

The Memory Process

  • Encoding: Information is processed into a form the brain can store.
  • Storage: Memories are retained until they are needed.
  • Retrieval: Stored information is recalled when required.

Why We Forget

  • Information was not encoded effectively.
  • New and old memories interfere with one another.
  • Lack of cues makes retrieval more difficult.
  • Memories naturally fade when they are not reinforced.

What Can Affect Memory?

  • Normal aging.
  • Poor sleep.
  • Stress, anxiety, or depression.
  • Head injuries or certain medical conditions.
  • Some medications and vitamin deficiencies.

Ways to Improve Memory

  • Exercise regularly.
  • Get enough quality sleep.
  • Stay mentally active by learning new skills.
  • Practice active recall and review information regularly.
  • Group information into meaningful chunks.
  • Reduce distractions while studying.
  • Connect new information to what you already know.
  • Eat a balanced diet that supports brain health.

Remember

Memory improves with attention, repetition, and healthy lifestyle habits. Regular mental stimulation, physical activity, quality sleep, and effective learning strategies can help keep your memory sharp throughout life.

title: What Is Short-Term Memory?
header: How long does short-term memory really last? Psychology reveals the answer
content:
Short-term memory (STM) temporarily stores a small amount of information, such as a phone number or a short list, while you actively use it. Without attention or repetition, the information is quickly forgotten.

Key Features of Short-Term Memory

  • Limited capacity: Most people can hold about 5 to 9 pieces of information at one time.
  • Short duration: Information typically lasts about 15 to 30 seconds unless it is rehearsed.
  • Temporary storage: STM acts as a mental workspace for everyday thinking and problem-solving.

Important Memory Theories

  • Miller's Theory: Proposed that short-term memory can hold about 7 ± 2 items.
  • Peterson and Peterson: Demonstrated that information fades rapidly from short-term memory without rehearsal.
  • Atkinson and Shiffrin: Introduced the Multi-Store Model, describing sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.
  • Baddeley and Hitch: Expanded the idea of short-term memory into the Working Memory Model, explaining how we actively process and use information.

How Rehearsal Helps

Repeating information, such as silently rehearsing a phone number, helps keep it active in short-term memory and increases the chance of transferring it to long-term memory.

Ways to Improve Short-Term Memory

  • Repeat important information.
  • Group information into meaningful chunks.
  • Focus your attention and reduce distractions.
  • Connect new information with what you already know.
  • Get enough sleep and practice regularly.

Remember

Short-term memory has limited time and capacity, but attention, repetition, and effective learning strategies can improve recall and support the formation of long-term memories.

  • Chronic stress: High levels of stress hormones over time can interfere with memory, learning, and concentration.
  • Poor sleep: Stress often disrupts sleep, making it harder for the brain to store and retrieve memories.

Ways to Protect Your Memory

Remember

title: Understanding Explicit Memory
header: Explore the hidden process your brain uses to store facts and life moments
content:
Memory allows you to learn, store, and recall information. Long-term memory includes explicit memory, which helps you consciously remember facts, knowledge, and personal experiences.

Types of Memory

  • Sensory memory: Briefly holds information from your senses.
  • Short-term memory: Temporarily stores a small amount of information for immediate use.
  • Long-term memory: Stores information for extended periods, sometimes for a lifetime.

What Is Explicit Memory?

Explicit memory is the conscious recall of information. It allows you to remember facts, names, places, and personal events whenever you need them.

  • Semantic memory: Stores general knowledge, such as facts, words, and concepts.
  • Episodic memory: Stores personal experiences and important life events.

How Memories Are Formed

  • Encoding: Information is processed into a form the brain can store.
  • Storage: The brain retains the information over time.
  • Retrieval: Stored memories are recalled when needed.

Ways to Strengthen Memory

Explicit memory helps you recall both facts and personal experiences. Healthy habits, regular mental stimulation, and consistent learning can strengthen memory and support long-term brain health.

title: Psychology of Confirmation Bias
header: Unlock the hidden bias that makes you ignore facts and trust your own opinions
content:
Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice, remember, and give more weight to information that supports our existing beliefs while overlooking evidence that challenges them. Recognizing this bias can help you make more balanced and informed decisions.

How Confirmation Bias Affects Us

  • Information seeking: We often look for sources that agree with our opinions.
  • Interpreting evidence: People can reach different conclusions from the same facts based on their existing beliefs.
  • Selective memory: We tend to remember information that confirms what we already think and forget information that does not.

Everyday Examples

  • Reading only news that matches your views.
  • Following social media accounts that reinforce your opinions.
  • Ignoring feedback that challenges your assumptions.
  • Remembering events in ways that support your perspective.

How to Reduce Confirmation Bias

  • Seek information from a variety of reliable sources.
  • Listen to different viewpoints with an open mind.
  • Ask yourself what evidence could change your opinion.
  • Question your assumptions before making important decisions.
  • Focus on facts rather than emotions or personal preferences.

Remember

Everyone experiences confirmation bias from time to time. Becoming aware of it helps you think more critically, evaluate evidence fairly, and make wiser decisions in everyday life.

title: Five Tips To A Better Sleep

content:

  • Give your body time to develop a regular sleep routine.

Remember

Better sleep is built through healthy daily habits. Staying active, limiting screen time before bed, maintaining a relaxing bedtime routine, and following a consistent sleep schedule can improve both your sleep quality and overall well-being.

title: Endowment Effect: Definition, What Causes It, and Example
header: Learn how this mental bias quietly affects your buying, selling, and decisions
content:
The endowment effect is a cognitive bias where people place a higher value on something simply because they own it. This can make it harder to make objective decisions about buying, selling, or letting go of possessions.

Why the Endowment Effect Happens

  • Ownership: We naturally feel more attached to things that belong to us.
  • Loss aversion: Giving something up often feels more painful than gaining something of equal value.
  • Emotional attachment: Personal memories or sentimental value can increase how much we value an item.

Everyday Examples

  • Refusing to sell an item because you believe it is worth more than buyers are willing to pay.
  • Keeping clothes, gadgets, or collectibles you rarely use because they feel too valuable to give away.
  • Holding onto investments longer than planned because selling feels like accepting a loss.

How to Reduce This Bias

  • Evaluate items based on their current value rather than your attachment to them.
  • Ask yourself what you would pay for the item if you did not already own it.
  • Use clear rules when making financial or purchasing decisions.
  • Consider objective information before deciding to keep or sell something.

Remember

The endowment effect affects everyone from time to time. Being aware of this bias can help you make more balanced financial decisions, reduce emotional decision-making, and judge the value of possessions more objectively.

title: The psychological reason most people overvalue things they already own
header: Find out how a hidden bias makes you think your stuff is worth more than it is
content:
The endowment effect is a cognitive bias that causes people to value something more simply because they own it. This emotional attachment can influence buying, selling, and everyday decision-making.

Why It Happens

  • Ownership: We naturally place greater value on things that belong to us.
  • Loss aversion: Giving up something we own often feels more painful than gaining something of equal value.
  • Emotional attachment: Personal experiences and memories can make possessions seem more valuable than their market price.

Everyday Examples

  • Pricing a used car or personal item higher than buyers think it is worth.
  • Keeping possessions you rarely use because they feel too valuable to let go.
  • Holding onto investments longer than planned because selling feels like a loss.

How to Make More Objective Decisions

  • Ask yourself what you would pay for the item if you did not already own it.
  • Compare your opinion with current market prices.
  • Separate emotional attachment from financial value.
  • Use clear rules when buying, selling, or investing.

Remember

The endowment effect is a common bias that affects everyone. Recognizing it can help you evaluate possessions more objectively, negotiate more effectively, and make better financial and personal decisions.

  • Practice self-compassion: Treat yourself with kindness instead of harsh self-criticism.
  • Use mindfulness: Deep breathing, meditation, or journaling can help calm a busy mind.

Remember

You cannot control every outcome, but you can control how you respond. By focusing on the present, challenging unhelpful thoughts, and taking small, meaningful steps forward, you can reduce overthinking and build greater confidence and peace of mind.
